opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that was a real turning point for me. Before then, I'd half-dismissed behavior cloning as the naive baseline. The textbook story is that you hit compounding errors and distribution shift: the policy drifts slightly off the demonstrations, ends up in states it has never seen, and falls apart. So a lot of us assumed the serious answer would come from reinforcement learning, or from very structured planning methods.

Seeing what the DeepMind folks, and a few other industry groups around that time, were getting out of what was essentially supervised learning on demonstrations really challenged that view. When you put enough care into data collection, with consistent teleoperation, diverse scenes, and lots of recovery behavior in the data, plus a reasonably expressive model, behavior cloning turned out to be far more capable than the theory suggested. It didn't solve everything, but the gap between "this shouldn't work" and "this works surprisingly well" told me our assumptions were off.

The bigger lesson for me was that the bottleneck had moved. It was less about the learning algorithm and more about the data: how you collect it, how much you have, how diverse it is, and whether it covers the failure modes. That changed what I wanted to work on. I became much more interested in scalable ways to gather demonstrations, in making imitation robust to imperfect or mixed-quality data, and in combining learned policies with structure like task decomposition or planning, so you aren't relying purely on brute-force data for long-horizon tasks.

It also made me more humble about the theory side. The compounding-error argument is real, but it's a worst-case story. In practice, with the right data distribution, you can push a long way before it bites. Figuring out exactly where that boundary sits, and what you need to go beyond it, is still one of the most interesting open questions to me.

r001.rationale: The candidate says seeing DeepMind’s results with supervised learning on demonstrations challenged his doubts and showed behavior cloning was more capable than expected.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So, I want to be careful here, because the honest answer is that it wasn't one single moment of seeing a demo and having my mind changed. It was more a slow shift in what I thought the bottleneck was.

When I was coming up, the dominant framing in the field was that behavior cloning is the naive baseline. You collect demonstrations, you fit a policy to them with supervised learning, and then everyone points at compounding errors and distribution shift and says, see, this doesn't work, you need reinforcement learning or some kind of interactive correction on top. And I believed that. I spent a lot of time on hierarchical methods and learning from play and ways to get more out of the data precisely because I assumed that plain imitation would hit a ceiling very quickly.

What I think the DeepMind robotics work did, especially the large-scale efforts where they were pooling data across many tasks and embodiments and just training big models on it, was make the case that a lot of what we were attributing to the algorithm was actually about scale and about data coverage. When you see a system that is, at its core, doing supervised learning on demonstrations, and it generalizes in ways that the small-data regime would never predict, you have to go back and ask whether the theoretical arguments against behavior cloning were really arguments about behavior cloning or arguments about having a few hundred trajectories.

So it reframed the question for me. Instead of asking how to replace imitation with something smarter, I started asking what the data distribution needs to look like for imitation to be enough, and where exactly it still breaks. And it does still break. Precision manipulation, long-horizon tasks, recovery from states that no human demonstrator ever visited. Those are real. But they now feel like data problems and representation problems rather than a fundamental flaw in the approach.

The other thing I'd say, and this is more of a cultural observation, is that it gave people permission to take the simple thing seriously. For a long time, if you submitted a paper that was essentially good behavior cloning with careful engineering, reviewers would say, where's the novelty. Seeing a group with that much credibility lean into it changed what the community was willing to consider a legitimate research direction. And I think that's been healthy, even if I'd push back on some of the more triumphalist takes about scaling solving everything.

r001.rationale: He says that seeing DeepMind’s systems use supervised learning on demonstrations and generalize changed his view, showing him that behavior cloning can work when data and scale are sufficient.

astra-6.text:
Seeing DeepMind’s robotics work made me take behavior cloning much more seriously. The idea is straightforward: collect demonstrations and train a policy to predict the actions. But seeing that approach produce actual robot behavior made me think, maybe we should understand how far this simple recipe can go before assuming we need something more complicated.

There’s still a fundamental challenge: once the robot makes a small mistake, it can end up in a situation that wasn’t represented in the demonstrations. So for me, the question became: what data do we need, and how do we get enough coverage for the robot to handle those situations?

r001.rationale: He says DeepMind’s work showed the approach producing actual robot behavior, which gave him evidence that behavior cloning works.

sol-6.1.text: Seeing DeepMind’s robotics work made me take behavior cloning much more seriously. There’s something very compelling about watching a robot learn a useful behavior directly from demonstrations. But it also highlights the central challenge: when the robot makes a small mistake, it can end up in a situation that wasn’t represented in the training data. So the question for me became, how do we move beyond reproducing demonstrations to learning policies that can recover and generalize?

r001.rationale: He says DeepMind’s work made him take behavior cloning more seriously and describes watching a robot learn useful behavior directly from demonstrations, conveying firsthand evidence that it works.
